statement: How a death enters a count of drug deaths depends on the country, the register and the period, so figures from different sources do not count the same thing, and studies that matched the same deaths across two sources found that they overlapped only partly. In US national statistics a drug overdose death is one whose underlying cause on the death certificate is coded to ICD-10 X40–X44 (unintentional), X60–X64 (suicide), X85 (assault) or Y10–Y14 (undetermined intent); deaths from long-term drug effects and from side effects of medicines taken as prescribed are left out. A drug counts as involved when the certifier, usually a medical examiner or coroner, wrote it anywhere on the certificate, unless the words around it say otherwise, and a death with several drugs is counted under each of them, so the 15 drug-specific counts for 2023 added up to 179,965 against 106,352 deaths (editors' arithmetic); the National Center for Health Statistics calls its drug counts minimums and says that the certificate cannot show which drug caused a death involving several (Garnett et al., 2026). ICD-10 codes put different drugs together (fentanyl and tramadol share one code; oxycodone, morphine and codeine share another): in Washington State in 2003–2010 one code covered 2,725 poisoning deaths whose certificates named oxycodone, morphine, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, codeine or just 'opiate', which only the certificate's words could separate (Ossiander, 2014). The certifier's words also decide whether and how a death is coded: a US consensus panel convened by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration notes that 'acute cocaine intoxication' is coded as a poisoning while 'cocaine use' or 'cocaine abuse' is coded as a mental and behavioural disorder (Goldberger et al., 2013), and 'drug overdose' with no drug named is coded as unspecified drugs (Slavova et al., 2015). The same panel separated deaths caused by a drug from deaths in which a drug was only detected, for example a man shot dead with a drug in his blood, who counts as a drug-detected death but not a drug-caused one (Goldberger et al., 2013). European registers differ again. Norway's Cause of Death Registry, under the European (EMCDDA, now EUDA) definition, counts only the underlying cause and the first contributing cause (Amundsen, 2017). In Sweden, a national selection counted a listed drug code anywhere on the certificate, the European selection only the underlying cause from a shorter list, and a forensic register any death in which an illegal drug, methadone, buprenorphine or fentanyl was found at forensic examination, whatever the certified cause (Fugelstad et al., 2020). In England and Wales, the Office for National Statistics counts a death under a specific opioid only when the coroner's conclusion names it (Chen et al., 2025). Who decides differs as well: certifying physicians in Sweden and Norway, coroners in England and Wales, medical examiners or coroners in the US, and, for Norway's second register, local and central police (Fugelstad et al., 2020; Amundsen, 2017; Chen et al., 2025; Garnett et al., 2026). Matching the same deaths across two sources, the strongest evidence on this question, showed partial overlap in three countries. In Norway in 2007–2009, the Cause of Death Registry (822 deaths) and the police registry (562) together covered 929 people, of whom 455 (49%) were in both; 367 were only in the cause-of-death count, 74 police-registry deaths had a certified cause outside the European definition, and 33 had no match (39% of them not Norwegian citizens, the rest with missing or wrong identity numbers). Deaths only in the cause-of-death count were older, more often certified as dependence or suicide, more often had morphine or codeine, methadone or other synthetic opioids rather than heroin as the first drug listed, less often had an autopsy and more often occurred in hospitals or other institutions; autopsies were recorded for 715 of the 822, and the author states that neither source gives the correct figure (Amundsen, 2017). In Sweden in 1994–2012, the certificate-based selection and the forensic toxicology register shared 4,238 of the 9,707 deaths in either, with 2,210 only in the toxicology register and 3,259 only in the certificate selection; among deaths in the toxicology register whose main drug was heroin, 96% were also in the certificate selection, against 23% where it was cannabis (THC). The authors conclude that comparing numbers or rates of drug deaths between countries misleads, while comparing trends is meaningful where investigation and certification have not changed, although they analysed no other country (Fugelstad et al., 2020). In New Mexico in 1995–1998, where the state medical investigator examines suspected drug deaths with a full autopsy and toxicology by policy, vital statistics and the medical investigator's records each held 1,046 of the 1,105 residents' poisoning deaths found in either, and 987 were in both. Of 59 deaths counted as poisonings only by vital statistics, 24 occurred in another state, 13 had never been reported to the medical investigator and 15 were natural deaths in the medical investigator's records (such as cirrhosis, sepsis or heart disease) that vital statistics coded as non-dependent drug use because the certificate said 'use' or 'abuse'; of 59 counted only by the medical investigator, 37 had been coded as natural deaths because poisoning was written only in Part II of the certificate, and 17 as other injuries (Landen et al., 2003). Wider local definitions add other deaths: of 70 deaths that a coroner-fed UK register counted as drug-related in Liverpool (deaths in 2004 and inquests in January to June 2005), the register itself placed 21 outside its category for people with a known history of problem drug use, 25 were not deaths from drug toxicity, and 15 were of people living elsewhere (Beynon et al., 2007). Around 2000 in England and Wales, as cited by Webb et al. (2003), coroners' verdicts of death from drug misuse numbered 605 (2000), the same register counted 1,296 drug-related deaths (2000) and the Office for National Statistics 2,943 deaths with drug poisoning as the underlying cause (1999). The linkage studies come from Norway, Sweden and one US state, the newest data are from 2012, and none comes from southern Europe. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: How is a death counted as a drug death? It depends on the country and on the list. In the US, a death counts when drug poisoning is the main cause on the death certificate, and every drug written on it is counted, so one death can count under several drugs. Some European lists count only the main cause; one Swedish list counted every death in which a drug was found in tests, whatever the cause. Doctors, coroners, medical examiners or police decide, depending on the place, and the words written on the certificate decide how it is counted. When researchers matched the same deaths on two lists, the lists did not fully agree: in Norway (2007 to 2009) about half of the people were on both lists, in Sweden (1994 to 2012) fewer than half, and in one US state (1995 to 1998) about 9 in 10. So counts from different countries or lists are not the same thing. These matching studies come from three places, and the newest data are from 2012.

Washington State 2003–2010: one code (T40.2) covered 2,725 deaths naming six terms (Ossiander, 2014). Linkage: Norway 2007–2009, 929 people, 455 (49%) in both registers, 367 (40%) cause-of-death register only, 74 (8%) police register with a cause outside the European definition, 33 (4%) unmatched (Amundsen, 2017). Sweden 1994–2012: 4,238 of 9,707 in both the certificate selection and the toxicology register, 2,210 toxicology only, 3,259 certificate only; capture of toxicology-register deaths by the certificate selection, heroin 96%, THC 23% (Fugelstad et al., 2020). New Mexico 1995–1998: 1,046 in each source, 987 in both, 1,105 in either (94.7% and 89.3%); discordant deaths 59 each way (Landen et al., 2003). Liverpool 2004–2005: of 70 register deaths, 21 outside the problem-drug-use category, 25 not from drug toxicity, 15 non-residents (Beynon et al., 2007). England and Wales, as cited: 605 coroners' verdicts (2000), 1,296 register deaths (2000), 2,943 ONS drug-poisoning deaths (1999) (Webb et al., 2003). No intervals; counts of linked records.

statement: In the places and years studied, official counts missed some drug deaths, mostly because the certificate or its codes named no drug, or not the drug a fuller review identified, and they also included some deaths that a fuller review did not count as drug deaths; how many in each direction depends on the place, the period and the yardstick used. Certificates that name no drug: in US death records for 1999–2015, 23.1% of 568,699 drug poisoning deaths of all intents had no specific drug identified (26.0% in 2008, 17.2% in 2015) (Ruhm, 2018), and 97,159 of 438,607 unintentional overdose deaths (22%) named none, from 0% in Washington DC to 50.8% in Pennsylvania in 2015 (Buchanich et al., 2018); in 2010, 9,429 of 38,329 overdose deaths (about a quarter) carried only the code for unspecified drugs (Slavova et al., 2015). These national records do not show which deaths had toxicology. By 2023 the share of US overdose deaths with no drug or drug-class code had fallen to 4.0%, from 12.3% in 2017 (Garnett et al., 2026, editors' arithmetic), so corrections for 1999–2015 should not be carried to later years. Two corrections assumed that deaths naming no drug involved opioids as often as similar deaths with a named drug: a statistical model raised national opioid-involved counts by 21% to 36% a year (33,091 to about 40,000 in 2015; Ruhm, 2018), and reallocation by state and year added about 70,000 unintentional opioid-related deaths over 1999–2015, 5,662 of them in 2015, doubling Pennsylvania's 2015 rate (Buchanich et al., 2018). Neither was checked against toxicology or case records, both can only add deaths, and the national range of 20% to 35% that a scoping review reports comes from one author's repeated analyses of the same records (Gutkind et al., 2025). Searching the words written on certificates recovers drug names that the codes merge, but not a drug that was never written (Ossiander, 2014; Garnett et al., 2026). Counts can also jump when recording practice changes: as a review reports, South Carolina's death rate from prescription-type opioids went from 4.7 to 9.3 per 100,000 between 2013 and 2014, mainly because certificates naming specific drugs rose from 57.7% to 94.4% once the state began collecting drug names (Slavova et al., 2019, second-hand). Studies that compared two counting methods for the same deaths, the strongest evidence here, found gaps in both directions. In the Stockholm area in 1985–1996, a selection of death certificates by drug codes held 761 (63%) of 1,212 deaths in an inventory that assessed each death individually (1,061 of them examined forensically); but the inventory also counted deaths of people with a history of drug use problems whatever the cause, including 151 hospital deaths, mainly HIV-related, under a third of which the certificate selection held, so not every death it missed was a missed poisoning. In the other direction, the certificate selection held 419 deaths that the inventory did not; the authors judged only 30 of them drug-related by the inventory's definition, the rest including drownings after taking medicines and deaths related to alcohol or medicines rather than illegal drugs. Its total (1,181) was therefore close to the inventory's while about a third of the individual deaths differed in each direction; a toxicology-based register held 317 of 454 inventory deaths in 1994–1996, and 43 of its own cases reflected medical treatment rather than illicit use (Fugelstad et al., 2020). In New Mexico in 1995–1998, vital statistics left out 37 deaths that the state medical investigator classed as poisonings (coded as natural deaths because poisoning was written only in Part II of the certificate) and included 15 that the medical investigator classed as natural deaths (coded as drug use because of the certificate's words) (Landen et al., 2003). In England and Wales in 2011–2022, the Office for National Statistics counted a death under a specific opioid only when the coroner's conclusion named it; in coroner-reported cases of a national programme on drug deaths, 29% (2011) to 36% (2022) of heroin or morphine deaths, and similar shares for other opioids, had an ambiguous cause such as multi-drug toxicity with the programme's toxicologist implicating the opioid, and applying those shares to the national counts, without linking the records, gave projected totals of which the official counts held 61% to 68% (13,471 heroin or morphine deaths against a projected 20,323); 96.8% of the programme's opioid-related deaths had several drugs detected (Chen et al., 2025). Heroin is a special case, covered in the answer on heroin deaths. Counts that take every drug written on a certificate as involved, and count a death under each drug, cannot show which drug caused a death involving several (Garnett et al., 2026); in US records for 1999–2015, 45% of unintentional deaths counted as opioid-related also carried another drug's code (Buchanich et al., 2018, editors' calculation). Registers of drug-related deaths also include deaths that were not direct overdoses: of 1,037 accidental deaths that coroners in England and Wales reported to a national register in 2000, the register's researchers judged 802 (77%) direct overdoses and the rest sudden events such as breathing in stomach contents (74), drug toxicity on top of a medical condition (112), injuries (31) and infections (18), without comparing them with official statistics (Webb et al., 2003). Definitions also leave deaths out: US overdose counts exclude long-term effects of drugs (Garnett et al., 2026), and the authors of a Liverpool study argue that the UK and European definitions of the time left out deaths from infections spread by injecting (Beynon et al., 2007). No study read here measured how often stimulants, cannabis or new psychoactive substances are missed or wrongly named on certificates; most of the evidence concerns US opioid deaths before 2016. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Do official counts miss drug deaths? In the places studied, some, mostly because the death certificate named no drug or a different drug. In US records from 1999 to 2015, about 23 in 100 drug poisoning deaths named no drug; by 2023 only about 4 in 100 named no drug or type of drug. Researchers who assumed that many of those deaths involved opioids added between a fifth and a third to the opioid count, but nobody checked these guesses against test results. When the same deaths were counted two ways, errors went both ways. statement: In the three places studied, official counts built from death certificates or coroners' conclusions named heroin in fewer deaths than a fuller review of the investigation files found (Maryland; Victoria, Australia) or a projection estimated (England and Wales), mainly because morphine (which heroin turns into in the body) or a general term such as mixed drug toxicity was written instead; the fuller reviews used their authors' own definitions, which partly counted heroin markers found in toxicology rather than a judgement that heroin caused the death, and in the one place that looked, a few deaths coded as heroin were judged not to be heroin deaths. In Maryland in 2012–2015, certificates written by the state's medical examiner named heroin in 1,130 overdose deaths, while a protocol built by the state's agencies, which also counted deaths with 6-monoacetylmorphine (a breakdown product of heroin) in toxicology, morphine together with quinine (described as a common heroin additive), or morphine or no named drug on the certificate together with scene evidence of heroin, found 2,182; because the protocol includes every certificate naming heroin, it could only add deaths. Of the 1,052 it added, the certificate named morphine in 804, no specific drug in 193 and another substance in 55. Certificates named heroin in 51.8% (95% CI 49.7 to 53.9) of the protocol's heroin deaths, rising from 45.7% in 2012 to 56.3% in 2015, and less often for people aged 55 or older (41.9%), for women (35.1%) and for Black women (25.9%); the authors note that some of the added deaths, including some of the 55, may not have been heroin deaths (Horon et al., 2018). In Victoria, Australia, in 2012–2013, 243 deaths met the authors' own heroin-attribution model applied to closed coroners' files (toxicology together with the circumstances; 6-acetylmorphine was detected in 180, so 63 rested on morphine findings and circumstances), and the national heroin code was missing from 82 of them, leaving the national count 78 lower (165). Of 191 deaths the coroner attributed to heroin, 37 were not coded as heroin, mostly because of the wording (a general cause with the drugs listed only in a database field, morphine written as the cause, or a complication such as brain injury from lack of oxygen written first); 34 of 39 deaths certified as due to morphine or another opioid and all 5 certified as general drug toxicity lacked the heroin code (coders gave it to the other 5 of these 44, although the coroner had not named heroin), and 20 deaths had no code at all. In the other direction, 4 deaths coded as heroin were judged by the model to have involved heroin only by coincidence (Stam et al., 2019). In England and Wales in 2011–2022, the Office for National Statistics counted 13,471 deaths in which the coroner's conclusion named heroin or morphine; in coroner-reported cases of a national programme on drug deaths, 29% (2011) to 36% (2022) of heroin or morphine deaths had an ambiguous cause with the toxicologist implicating the drug, and applying these shares to the national counts, without linking the records, projects about 20,323, about half as many again (editors' calculation); the median number of drugs detected in these deaths rose from four to six (Chen et al., 2025). A scoping review reports, second-hand, similar shifts in US county reviews: in Allegheny County in 2008–2010, heroin deaths rose from 171 to 245 after review while deaths attributed to morphine fell from 132 to 41 and to codeine from 34 to 5, and in New York City in 2006–2010, 84 of 118 deaths certified as acute opiate intoxication were attributed to heroin (Gutkind et al., 2025). Why heroin is missed, as the authors describe it from the literature: heroin turns quickly into 6-acetylmorphine and then into morphine, so morphine found after death may come from heroin or from morphine itself, and 6-acetylmorphine may not be found after a long interval between use and death or in stored samples (Stam et al., 2019; Horon et al., 2018). US national statistics note that morphine on certificates may reflect heroin, which would understate heroin and overstate morphine (Garnett et al., 2026), and a US medical examiners' position paper treats 6-acetylmorphine as sufficient evidence of heroin and a morphine-to-codeine ratio above 1 as possible evidence, without a cited test of these rules (Davis et al., 2020). None of these studies checked its fuller review against an independent standard, and all concern 2006–2022; whether the deaths added by the reviews were caused by heroin, rather than involving it, is not shown, and what an opioid level after death can show is a separate question. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Do official counts miss heroin deaths? In three places studied, official counts named heroin less often than closer checks suggested. Heroin turns into morphine in the body, so morphine is often found after death, and certificates often said morphine or 'mixed drugs' instead of heroin. In Maryland (2012 to 2015), certificates named heroin in about 1,100 deaths, while a fuller check found about 2,200. In Victoria, Australia (2012 to 2013), the official heroin code was missing from 82 of 243 deaths a fuller check linked to heroin, and a few deaths coded as heroin were judged not to be heroin deaths. In England and Wales (2011 to 2022), one estimate made without matching records suggests about half as many again as official counts showed. The fuller checks used their own rules, partly based on heroin traces found in tests, and nobody checked those rules against an independent standard.

statement: A full autopsy with drug testing changed which deaths were counted as drug deaths in both directions at the one US centre that measured it, and access to testing differs widely between offices, but no study read here measured the effect on official counts. At a regional autopsy centre serving 33 counties of western North Carolina (population 2,354,038), which kept doing full autopsies on suspected drug deaths in 2016–2021 when other offices had moved to an external examination with toxicology, investigators suspected before autopsy that 2,719 of 2,956 adult deaths were drug-related, from drug equipment at the scene, a history of substance use disorder or earlier overdoses. After full autopsy and comprehensive toxicology, the assigned pathologist gave a cause unrelated to drugs in 265 of them (9.75%), for example a blood clot in the lungs, a burst stomach ulcer, a burst brain aneurysm with no stimulants in the body, or a bleed pressing on the brain in a homicide. Because the 265 include deaths whose toxicology found no drug, which a toxicology test alone would also have flagged, 9.75% is an upper limit for what an external examination with toxicology would have put down to drugs wrongly; the paper does not give the split. In the other direction, 115 of the 237 deaths not suspected (48.5%, editors' calculation) were given a drug-related cause. The pathologist's conclusion was the yardstick, illicit drugs found were counted as at least contributing unless a catastrophic natural or traumatic cause was found, and suicides, deaths with obvious fatal injuries and people under 18 were left out (Hancock et al., 2024). The National Association of Medical Examiners recommends a full autopsy whenever intoxication is suspected (except deaths after a hospital stay) and comprehensive toxicology for eight kinds of death; it states that history, investigation and autopsy together are an insensitive guide to intoxication and that no peer-reviewed study has shown an external examination to be as accurate as an autopsy, but its figure of 20% to 30% wrong diagnoses without autopsy comes from general autopsy studies, some decades old, not from drug deaths (Davis et al., 2020, a position paper). Access to testing varies: in the 2018 census of US medical examiner and coroner offices, of 1,320 offices that answered, 82.6% had access to toxicology (5.9% in-house, 76.7% through outside laboratories), 11.2% had none and 6.2% said they did not need it; 96.4% of offices serving 250,000 people or more had access, against 75.1% of those serving fewer than 25,000; coroners or other non-physicians most often decided which deaths were tested (64.7%); 53.9% of offices used drug screening tests and 95.1% of these confirmed them in a laboratory; and the authors state that the number of suspected overdose deaths actually tested is not known (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025). In surveillance records of 55,430 drug poisoning deaths in nine US states in 2019–2021, an autopsy was recorded for about 67%, an opioid test for 79% and an alcohol test for 76%, with 'not done' and 'unknown' counted together (Lundberg et al., 2026). What is tested changes what is found: as a review reports, routine testing for gabapentin in Kentucky from July 2014 raised its share among overdose deaths from 2.9% to 17% (Slavova et al., 2019, second-hand), and a US consensus panel notes that common screening tests miss some opioids, such as oxycodone and hydromorphone, and that laboratories use no standard thresholds (Goldberger et al., 2013). Of 48 of Kentucky's 120 elected coroners who answered a survey in 2016, after state laws of 2012 and 2015 required toxicology testing, 58% said they requested more toxicology testing and 35% more autopsies, as they reported it (Quesinberry et al., 2019). In Norway in 2007–2009, deaths counted by the cause-of-death register but not by the police were less often autopsied (odds ratio 2.66 for no autopsy) (Amundsen, 2017), and in Stockholm in 1994–1996 a register built from forensic toxicology could not include deaths without a forensic examination, such as the 151 hospital deaths in the reference inventory (Fugelstad et al., 2020). How often deaths certified without autopsy or testing are wrongly put down to drugs, or missed, has not been measured in official statistics. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Do autopsies and drug tests change which deaths count as drug deaths? At one autopsy centre in North Carolina (2016 to 2021), investigators suspected that 2,719 deaths were drug deaths. After a full autopsy and drug tests, about 1 in 10 of them had another cause, such as a blood clot or a burst blood vessel in the brain. This is an upper limit, because it includes deaths where tests found no drug at all. Of 237 deaths nobody suspected, about half turned out to be drug deaths. Testing differs a lot: in 2018, about 1 in 9 US death investigation offices had no access to drug testing, and small offices had it less often than big ones. Medical examiners' guidance says to do a full autopsy whenever a drug death is suspected, but the error figure it gives comes from autopsy studies of all kinds of deaths. This rests mainly on one centre in one US state.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether the kind of official who investigates a death changes how drug deaths are counted. In the US, counties served by coroners recorded drug deaths less specifically than counties served by medical examiners in the same states, but the one study of states that replaced coroners with medical examiners found no detectable improvement in how specifically poisoning deaths were coded, and across nine states taken together, without allowing for the state, the association ran the other way; no study checked which records were right. In the US, medical examiners are appointed physicians, usually forensic pathologists, while coroners are elected or appointed officials whose qualifications vary widely (Goldberger et al., 2013). In Kentucky, for example, a coroner must be at least 24 years old and meet residence rules, no training in medicine or forensic pathology is required, and new coroners must complete 40 hours of basic training; of 48 coroners who answered a 2016 survey, 47 held another job, 28 as funeral directors (Quesinberry et al., 2019). In the 2018 census of US offices, about 80% were in coroner systems, coroners or other non-physicians most often decided which deaths were tested (64.7%), and offices serving fewer than 25,000 people less often had access to toxicology (75.1%, against 96.4% of offices serving 250,000 or more) (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025). In surveillance records of 55,430 drug poisoning deaths in nine states in 2019–2021, deaths in coroner counties had higher odds of being recorded as of undetermined intent, rather than as an accident or a suicide, than deaths in medical-examiner counties of the same state and year (odds ratio 1.79, 95% CI 1.43 to 2.27; 1.52 to 1.61 after allowing for county characteristics, recorded investigation steps and the person's age, sex and race); without allowing for the state the odds were lower in coroner counties (0.32; 3.1% against 8.9% recorded as undetermined), which the authors attribute to Maryland, a state with a central medical examiner and many undetermined deaths. An alcohol test was recorded for 58.6% of deaths in coroner counties against 84.5% in medical-examiner counties, while autopsies (about 68% and 67%) and opioid tests (about 80% and 79%) were recorded about equally often (editors' percentages); the type of system was taken from a 2024 listing (Lundberg et al., 2026). A scoping review summarizes, second-hand, three studies that found more certificates naming no drug where coroners certify, one with odds ratios of 1.77 (2014) and 3.87 (2018) for an unclassified overdose death in coroner counties (Gutkind et al., 2025); a commentary quotes an earlier analysis in which 92% of overdose certificates named drugs in states with a central medical examiner, against 62% in states with coroners (Slavova et al., 2015, as cited); and a 2019 review reports that Maryland, a central medical-examiner state, recorded 68% of poisoning deaths as of undetermined intent in 2016, against 1% in Connecticut and Massachusetts (Slavova et al., 2019, as cited). Against this, seven states that switched to a medical examiner system in 1976–1996, compared with seven states that did not, chosen for nearness and similar earlier trends, showed no detectable change in the share of poisoning deaths with a non-specific underlying-cause code (difference-in-differences −0.02 to −0.03, standard errors 0.04 to 0.06, so falls of up to 10 to 14 percentage points from a share near one half could not be ruled out, editors' calculation), in data that ended in 1998 and included poisonings by substances other than drugs (Zaychik, 2024). See the contested question. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does it matter whether a coroner or a medical examiner investigates? It is not clear. In the US, medical examiners are doctors; coroners are often elected, and in some states need no medical training. In nine US states (2019 to 2021), deaths in coroner areas were more often recorded without saying whether the death was an accident or a suicide than deaths in medical examiner areas of the same state. Other studies found that certificates named no drug more often where coroners work. But seven states that switched to medical examiners showed no clear change in how precisely poisoning deaths were recorded, although that study could not rule out a real improvement, and its data end in 1998. Nobody checked which records were right.

debate.question: When a coroner rather than a medical examiner investigates, are drug deaths counted differently or less accurately, and would switching systems change the counts?
debate.evidence_yes: In surveillance records of 55,430 drug poisoning deaths in nine US states in 2019–2021, deaths in coroner counties had higher odds of being recorded as of undetermined intent than deaths in medical-examiner counties of the same state and year (odds ratio 1.79, 95% CI 1.43 to 2.27), and the estimate stayed between 1.52 and 1.61 after allowing for county size, poverty, unemployment, rurality, recorded autopsy and toxicology, suicide notes, investigator narratives and the person's age, sex and race; alcohol tests were recorded less often in coroner counties (58.6% against 84.5%) (Lundberg et al., 2026). A scoping review summarizes three studies that found more certificates naming no drug where coroners certify, one with odds ratios of 1.77 (2014) and 3.87 (2018), with unclassified deaths falling faster in medical-examiner counties (72% against 43%, 2014–2018) and lower odds where the certifier is a pathologist, coroners must be trained or the system is centralized (Gutkind et al., 2025, second-hand). An earlier analysis quoted in a commentary found that 92% of overdose certificates named drugs in states with a central medical examiner, against 62% in coroner states (Slavova et al., 2015, as cited). Coroners in some states need no medical training (Kentucky; Quesinberry et al., 2019), and in 2018 about 80% of US offices were in coroner systems, coroners or other non-physicians most often decided which deaths were tested, and small offices less often had access to toxicology (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025).
debate.evidence_no: The only before-and-after test found no detectable improvement: in seven US states that replaced coroners or justices of the peace with medical examiners in 1976–1996, compared with seven comparison states that did not, the share of poisoning deaths with a non-specific underlying-cause code did not fall detectably more after the switch (difference-in-differences −0.02 to −0.03) (Zaychik, 2024). Across the nine states taken together, without allowing for the state, deaths in coroner counties were less often recorded as undetermined (3.1% against 8.9%; odds ratio 0.32), which the authors attribute to Maryland, a central medical-examiner state (Lundberg et al., 2026); Maryland recorded 68% of poisoning deaths as undetermined in 2016, against 1% in Connecticut and Massachusetts (Slavova et al., 2019, as cited), so a medical-examiner system can record drug deaths very unspecifically. In the nine-state data, autopsies and opioid tests were recorded about as often in coroner as in medical-examiner counties (editors' percentages; Lundberg et al., 2026).
debate.neither_can_show: No study checked, against an independent review of the same deaths, which recorded intent or drug was correct, so 'undetermined' or 'no drug named' measures how specifically deaths were recorded, not how many were missed or wrongly attributed. Comparisons between counties cannot separate the type of office from what usually comes with it (budget, staff, caseload, access to toxicology, rurality, state law), some of which is part of what a system is; the nine-state study took each county's system from a 2024 listing for deaths in 2019–2021 and combined two surveillance systems by manner of death. The before-and-after study had seven switches, all before 1999, used underlying-cause codes that mix drug and non-drug poisonings, did not allow for repeated years of the same state, and was too imprecise to rule out falls of 10 to 14 percentage points. The 92% and 62% figures and the county odds ratios are second-hand and unadjusted or not appraised here.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In the US studies read, deaths investigated in coroner-served areas tended to be recorded less specifically, with no drug named more often and, within states, more often as of undetermined intent, than deaths investigated by medical examiners. Whether that is caused by the type of office, or by the smaller budgets, scarcer testing and officials without medical training that often come with it, is not known, and the only test of a change of system, with data before 1999, could neither show nor rule out an improvement. Maryland shows that a central medical-examiner system can also record many drug deaths as undetermined, so rules and practice within a state matter as well as the title of the office. None of this shows how many drug deaths either system misses or wrongly counts.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Before-and-after studies of recent changes of system or of rules (such as toxicology mandates or certifier training) in the ICD-10 era, with drug-specific outcomes (the share of certificates naming each drug and the share recorded as undetermined), matched comparison areas, enough cases and standard errors that allow for repeated years of the same area; and linkage of certificates in both kinds of system with an independent review of the same deaths, blinded to the type of office, recording each office's budget, staffing and testing, to measure missed and wrongly attributed deaths in both directions.

statement: In one randomized online experiment with UK adults, details in a simulated news report of a drug death changed how much stigma readers said they felt towards the person who died, by small to moderate amounts, but hardly changed their stated support for harm-reduction policies. In June 2022, 1,248 adults on a UK online research panel (Prolific; mean age 45.7, 51.0% women) were each randomly assigned to read one of eight versions of a BBC-style news story about an inquest, adapted from a real 2019 report of an ecstasy death; the versions differed in the person's gender (Jane or John), age together with use history (21 and had used the drug 'once or twice', or 43 and had used it regularly for 15 years) and drug (ecstasy or heroin). Stigma towards the person, on a new nine-item measure of blame, anger, pity, responsibility, control and wish for distance (range 9 to 81), was higher when the person was a man (mean 45.6 against 43.4 for a woman), when the person was older with long use (46.7 against 42.3) and when the drug was heroin (46.9 against 42.1): about 0.2, 0.4 and 0.4 standard deviations (editors' calculation), with the eight versions ranging from 38.6 (young woman, ecstasy) to 50.1 (older man, heroin). Support for six harm-reduction policies (such as drug checking, drug consumption rooms, take-home naloxone and opioid agonist treatment; range 6 to 30) was slightly higher after the older person's story (about 23.6 against 23.0, editors' calculation from the condition means, about 0.1 standard deviation; the paper prints the two means in reverse order), a difference seen in the ecstasy stories only, and did not differ by drug or by gender. In exploratory, non-randomized analyses of 868 participants, stronger belief in a just world, less perspective-taking and more general stigma towards people with drug problems went with more stigma towards the person, and having seen media coverage of a family affected by a drug death went with less (Sumnall et al., 2023). The study was not registered in advance, the stigma measure was new, the panel was matched to the UK population on sex, age and ethnicity only and over-represented people with degrees and people who prefer left-wing parties, the outcomes were self-reports measured once straight after one written story, and 'older' cannot be separated from 'longer use'. How real news coverage affects behaviour, policy or the people affected was not studied. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Does how the news describes a drug death change what readers think? In one UK study, 1,248 adults online each read one made-up news story about a drug death, with the details chosen at random. Readers judged the person more harshly when the person who died was a man, was 43 and had used the drug for years rather than 21 and trying it, and when the drug was heroin rather than ecstasy. These were small to moderate differences. Support for services that reduce harm, such as drug checking, barely changed. Readers saw one made-up story and answered straight away; the study did not look at what they did later, and it could not tell the effect of age apart from the effect of using drugs for longer.

statement: In the UK mephedrone scare of 2009–2010, several deaths that online news linked to mephedrone were later reported not to have been caused by it, including the deaths most linked to it online; the evidence is one study of online news whose later toxicology comes second-hand from press reports of inquests, so its figures are illustrative. Searching Google News from 26 November 2009 to one year after the ban (enforced on 16 April 2010), the author found 18 named people whose deaths online news linked to mephedrone; suicides and violent or accidental deaths were left out, and their number is not given. Later press reports said that mephedrone was not found in 4, including two young men in Scunthorpe, whose names were linked to mephedrone on about 9,060 and 8,730 web pages by June 2011 (more than any other case), who were reported a month after the ban not to have taken mephedrone, and whose inquest in 2011 found that they died from alcohol combined with methadone; that it was found but was not a factor in 4; and that it was a factor in 7, six of them with other drugs or illnesses also alleged. For 3 there was no later toxicology note, and the first death linked to mephedrone, of a 14-year-old girl in November 2009, was reported in local news within a month as due to natural causes (pneumonia after a streptococcal infection), yet went on being named as a mephedrone death in local, national and international news for months. The author reads the volume of news as showing that reports confirming that mephedrone was not responsible were far fewer than the earlier reports suggesting that it was. Relative Google searches for 'mephedrone', and for 'mephedrone buy', rose around the most-reported deaths and fell after the ban; these are screenshots of relative search volume without numbers, and the author concedes that a search is not a purchase, so they do not show that the news made people seek or use the drug (Forsyth, 2012). For comparison, the paper cites official statistics recording 6 drug-related deaths involving mephedrone, confirmed by toxicology, among 2,747 drug-related deaths in England and Wales in 2010, 2 of them with mephedrone as the only drug found (as cited by Forsyth, 2012). The 18 deaths are the media's selection, not a count of deaths involving mephedrone, and the outcome of each comes from newspapers rather than coroners' records; how many deaths blamed on mephedrone were confirmed in national registers is in the answer on confirmed mephedrone deaths. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Did news stories about mephedrone deaths get the facts right? Not always. In 2009 and 2010, online news in the UK linked 18 named deaths to mephedrone. Later newspaper reports said mephedrone was not found in 4 of them, was found but did not cause the death in 4, and played a part in 7, mostly together with other drugs or illnesses. The two deaths most linked to mephedrone online were later found to be from alcohol and methadone, and the first death in the news was reported as natural causes within a month. Online searches for mephedrone rose when deaths were in the news, but this does not show that the news made people use it. This comes from one study, and the later test results come from newspaper reports, not official records.

outcome: Whether mephedrone was later reported to have caused the deaths linked to it in the news; relative online search interest around the reports
magnitude: Forsyth (2012), 18 named deaths linked to mephedrone in online news (26 November 2009 to about April 2011; suicides and violent or accidental deaths excluded, number not given). Later press reports: not detected 4; detected, not a factor 4; detected and a factor 7 (6 with other drugs or conditions alleged); no toxicology note 3 (one reported as natural causes); editors' tally of Table 1 notes. Most-linked cases: 9,060 and 8,730 web pages (Scunthorpe; alcohol and methadone at inquest). Cited from ONS: 6 toxicologically confirmed mephedrone-related deaths among 2,747 drug-related deaths, England and Wales, 2010; mephedrone the only drug in 2. Search data relative only, no numbers.

evidence.locator: Methods, 2nd to 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Google News was used to read in date order all online news about mephedrone from 26/11/09 until one year after the ban and to identify all UK mephedrone deaths reported online; Google Advanced Search counted web pages for each death ('Mephedrone AND [name]'); Google Trends and Insights gave search volume for 'mephedrone' and 'mephedrone buy'. Limitations stated: one search engine; Google News uses sources it selects (it says about 4500 English-language news sites); Trends values are normalised to the highest volume, so they give relative, not absolute, numbers.

evidence.locator: Findings › Measuring the time-line of a virtual drug scare, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 201) and 8th, 10th, 13th and 14th paragraphs (pp. 201–202)
evidence.extracted: The first death linked to mephedrone in the press (a 14-year-old girl, November 2009) was reported within a month in local online newspapers as due to natural causes (bronchopneumonia after a streptococcal A infection, according to the pathologist's report as quoted), while earlier accounts stayed online and local, national and international titles went on naming her as a mephedrone death for months. On 16–17 March 2010 a story attributed the deaths of two young men in Scunthorpe to mephedrone; press campaigns for a ban followed and the drug was banned (enforced 16/04/10); on 18/05/10 it was reported that the two had not used mephedrone, and an inquest in 2011 found they died from a combination of alcohol and methadone.

evidence.extracted: From the screenshots, searches for 'mephedrone' rose after the first death report and again after the Scunthorpe story, the rise in searches for 'mephedrone buy' after the Scunthorpe deaths dwarfed that after the first death, and searches for 'mephedrone' and news fell after the ban to levels comparable with those before the scare (no 'mephedrone buy' screenshot after 24 March 2010); values are normalised indices without absolute numbers. The author concedes that a search for 'mephedrone buy' does not mean an intent to buy or that coverage led to use, and that Google Trends show neither how many searched nor why, but reads the figures as suggesting a 'boomerang effect'. He reads the news-volume line as showing that news confirming that mephedrone was not responsible was much smaller than the earlier speculation.

grade.reasoning: A case series of deaths named in the news, starting low as observational evidence; down one for risk of bias and one for imprecision: very low. The claim rests only on this case series, whose toxicology is second-hand from newspapers, so it stays at draft and says its figures are illustrative (brief; METHODS §6.3). The search-interest findings are co-occurrence in screenshots and are reported as not showing cause, as the author concedes. Status single study; the project's reading list found no other study comparing news reports of individual drug deaths with later inquest or toxicology findings. The national register series of deaths blamed on mephedrone is a separate answer.
